draft.title: Effectiveness of the law for Indigenous peoples
card: To judge how effective a law is, ask whether it met its aims and whether it changed outcomes in people's lives. A law can succeed on one measure and fall short on another.
Native title law recognised that Indigenous peoples hold rights to land under their own laws and customs. This rejected the idea that Australia was empty land before 1788.
Gaps remain in health, in justice outcomes such as imprisonment rates, and in recognition. Legal change has not always led to change in everyday outcomes.
A balanced judgement names what the law has achieved, names the gaps that remain, and links the two. For example, native title is recognised, but claims can be slow and hard to prove.
draft.remember: Judge a law by its aims and its real outcomes, and weigh both achievements and gaps.

a.q: Which statement gives the most balanced judgement of the law's effectiveness for Indigenous peoples?
opts: Native title is a real gain, but health and justice gaps remain
Native title is a real gain, so no gaps in outcomes remain
Health and justice gaps show the law has achieved nothing
A law cannot be judged until every gap has been closed
a.why: A balanced judgement names both an achievement and a continuing gap. The second option ignores gaps that the card says remain. The third ignores real achievements such as native title.
a.clue: Look for the answer that names both a gain and a gap.

b.q: A student argues that a law is ineffective because Indigenous imprisonment rates are still far higher than for other Australians. What is the best response?
opts: The rates are a real gap, but the law's gains must be weighed too
The rates are not a fair measure of how any law is working
The rates do not matter, as the law was passed by Parliament
The rates are no problem, because native title is recognised
b.why: A law can succeed on one measure and fall short on another. Imprisonment rates are a real gap, but a full judgement also weighs achievements. Native title does not cancel the gap, so the last option is tempting but wrong.
b.clue: A fair judgement uses more than one measure.

proposal.title: Effectiveness of the law for Indigenous peoples
card: To judge how effective a law is, ask whether it met its aims and whether it changed outcomes in people's lives. A law can succeed on one measure and fall short on another.
The law has made real gains, such as the legal recognition of native title and laws against racial discrimination, such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.
Gaps remain in health, such as lower life expectancy, in justice outcomes such as imprisonment rates, and in recognition, as the Constitution does not recognise Indigenous peoples.
A balanced judgement names the gains, names the gaps, and weighs them together. One gain does not cancel out a gap, and a gap does not erase a gain.
proposal.remember: Weigh what the law has achieved against the gaps that still remain.

a.q: Which statement gives the most balanced judgement of the law's effectiveness for Indigenous peoples?
opts: Native title is a gain, but health and justice gaps remain
Native title is a gain, so the other gaps no longer matter
Health and justice gaps mean native title achieved nothing
Gaps remain, so the law cannot be judged until they close
a.why: A balanced judgement weighs a real gain alongside the gaps that remain. The statement that native title means the other gaps no longer matter is tempting, but one gain does not cancel out a gap. Saying the gaps mean nothing was achieved makes the opposite mistake.
a.clue: Can a law succeed and fall short at the same time?

The rates are no problem, because native title is recognised

b.clue: A fair judgement uses more than one measure.
